papers.title: Claw-free difference graphs of finite groups
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27414v1

summary.one_liner: The paper classifies finite groups whose difference graph (a graph built from cyclic subgroup relations among elements in the enhanced power graph) is claw-free, giving group-theoretic conditions, consequences for symmetric, alternating and simple groups, and a complete list for soluble groups.
summary.plain: The paper studies a graph built from a finite group: elements are linked when they generate a cyclic subgroup and neither is a power of the other. It asks when this graph contains no "claw" (one vertex joined to three others that are mutually unlinked). The authors show this happens exactly when the element orders and the centralizers of elements of order 2 and 3 satisfy specific restrictions, and they work out which groups qualify.
summary.why: The result gives a complete, checkable criterion linking a graph-theoretic property to the internal structure of groups, and it covers symmetric, alternating, simple and soluble groups. The text does not say what wider applications it has, so its significance beyond this graph-theoretic setting is unclear from the excerpt.
summary.background:
- A finite group: a finite set of symmetries closed under composition, such as permutations of n objects.
- Element order: the smallest positive power of an element that gives the identity.
- Cyclic group: a group generated by one element, like repeated rotation.
- Graph, vertex, edge: dots and lines; a claw is one dot joined to three dots that are not joined to each other.
- Enhanced power graph: the graph where elements are linked if they lie in a common cyclic subgroup; the difference graph is a refinement of it.
- Centralizer: the elements that commute with a given element.
- Sylow p-subgroup, normal subgroup, soluble group, simple group, EPPO group: standard group-theory terms; soluble groups are built from abelian pieces, and simple groups have no nontrivial normal subgroups.
- Frobenius group: a group with a complement acting fixed-point-freely on a normal subgroup.

papers.abstract: Let $\D(G)$ be the difference graph of a finite group $G$: the graph on the non-isolated vertices of $\PE(G)-\Pg(G)$, where $x\sim_{\D} y$ if and only if $\gen{x,y}$ is cyclic and neither of $x,y$ lies in the cyclic group generated by the other. A claw is the graph $K_{1,3}$ and a graph is claw-free if it has no induced claw. We prove that for every finite group $G$, $\D(G)$ is claw-free if and only if it is a disjoint union of copies of the path $P_3$, if and only if the element orders of $G$ are prime powers or $6$, every element of order $3$ has at most one involution in its centralizer, and every involution has at most one subgroup of order $3$ in its centralizer (equivalently: $C_G(a)$ has a normal Sylow $2$-subgroup of order at most $2$ for every $a$ of order $3$, and $C_G(u)$ a normal Sylow $3$-subgroup of order at most $3$ for every involution $u$). Consequences: a nilpotent group that is not a $p$-group has claw-free $\D$ if and only if $G\cong C_6$; $\D(\Sym_n)$ is claw-free if and only if $n\le 5$; $\D(\Alt_n)$ is claw-free if and only if $n\le 6$; a non-abelian simple group has claw-free $\D$ if and only if it is EPPO or $\PSL_2(11)$ or $\PSL_2(13)$, proved family by family (this uses the classification of finite simple groups). For soluble groups we obtain a complete classification: the non-EPPO soluble groups with claw-free $\D$ are $C_6$, $D_{12}$, $C_3\rtimes C_4$ and the Frobenius groups $N\rtimes K$ with $N$ an abelian $r$-group, $r\ge 5$, and $K\cong C_6$ or $C_3\rtimes C_4$. For every group with claw-free non-empty $\D$ we show $|O_2(G)|\le 2$ and $|O_3(G)|\le 3$, and we give non-soluble examples ($\Sym_5$, $\PGL_2(7)$, $\PSL_2(11)$, $\PSL_2(13)$). We also prove that the full enhanced power graph is claw-free only for cyclic groups and clarify the relations between claw-freeness of $\D(G)$, $\Pg(G)$ and $\PE(G)$.

papers.title: Local cohomology module with infinitely many associated primes over ramified regular local rings of the least possible dimensions
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26655v1

summary.one_liner: The paper constructs local cohomology modules with infinitely many associated primes over ramified regular local rings in two specific ring dimensions, which are the smallest possible, building on an earlier 12-dimensional example and a cited theorem (Theorem 2.6 in SS).
summary.plain: This paper is about a question in commutative algebra, a branch of mathematics that studies rings of polynomial-like objects. The author asks when certain algebraic objects called local cohomology modules can have infinitely many "associated primes," which are special sub-objects that record their structure. The paper builds such examples in two different dimensions of a particular kind of ring, and it says these dimensions are the least possible.
summary.why: Finding the smallest dimension where a behaviour occurs tells us where the boundary of the phenomenon lies. The text does not say how far the results reach beyond these examples, and it does not discuss applications outside algebra.
summary.background:
- Ring: a set of numbers or objects with addition and multiplication, such as polynomials.
- Regular local ring: a well-behaved ring with a single special point, where the "dimension" counts independent directions.
- Ramified: a technical condition on how the ring sits relative to a prime number; here it means the ring is not in the simplest form.
- Local cohomology module: an algebraic object built from a ring and an ideal (a special subset), used to measure its hidden structure.
- Associated prime: a special sub-object that a module "points to"; having infinitely many is unusual, since most modules of this kind have finitely many.
- Dimension: the number of independent directions in the ring.
- The text relies on an earlier result (SS, Theorem 2.6) and on an earlier paper (Ma) that gave a 12-dimensional example; the source of the cited theorem is not given here.

papers.abstract: In \cite{Ma} we have observed the example of local cohomology module with infinitely many associated primes over a 12 dimensional ramified regular local ring. In this paper we construct examples of local cohomology modules with infinitely many associated primes over ramified regular local rings of two different ring dimensions. The result of this paper is very much dependent on the result (\cite{SS}, Theorem 2.6).

papers.title: On coherence of enveloping algebras of infinite-dimensional Lie algebras
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27824v1

summary.background:
- Lie algebra: a vector space with a bracket operation, used to describe continuous symmetries.
- Universal enveloping algebra U(g): a ring built from a Lie algebra g that encodes its representations.
- Loop algebra: functions from a circle (or Laurent polynomials) with values in a finite-dimensional Lie algebra.
- Witt algebra: the derivations of Laurent polynomials, an infinite-dimensional example.
- Coherent ring: a ring where finitely generated one-sided ideals are finitely presented; a finiteness property.
- Noetherian ring: every ideal is finitely generated; coherence is a weaker related condition.
- Nilpotent: a Lie algebra whose repeated brackets eventually vanish.
- Graded and filtered rings: rings split into pieces indexed by integers or ordered by a size-like filtration; the Rees ring links the two.
summary.one_liner: The paper determines when universal enveloping algebras of infinite-dimensional Lie algebras (notably loop algebras and the Witt algebra) are coherent, and studies coherence of related graded and filtered rings.
summary.plain: The paper studies a property called "coherence" for a family of algebraic structures built from infinite-dimensional symmetry-like objects (Lie algebras). Coherence is a tidy-behaviour condition: roughly, certain systems of equations have solutions that are finitely described. The authors show that for loop algebras the property holds exactly when the underlying finite-dimensional algebra is nilpotent, and they find that several specific examples fail it.
summary.why: It sharpens what is known about which infinite-dimensional algebras behave well under standard finiteness conditions, and it extends earlier work on non-Noetherianity of the Witt-algebra enveloping algebra. The text does not indicate further applications beyond this algebraic classification.

papers.abstract: We investigate when the universal enveloping algebra $U(\mathfrak{g})$ of an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ is coherent. We show that if $\mathfrak{g}$ is the loop algebra of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{h}$ then $U(\mathfrak{g})$ is coherent exactly when $\mathfrak{h}$ is nilpotent. As a consequence, we show that $U(\mathfrak{g})$ is not coherent if $\mathfrak{g}$ is complex, simple, $\mathbb{Z}$-graded, of polynomially bounded growth, and not isomorphic to the Witt algebra $W = \mathrm{Der} \mathbb{C}[t,t^{-1}]$ or its one-sided version. We also demonstrate that the homomorphic image of $U(W)$ used to prove non-Noetherianity of $U(W)$ in previous work of the first author and Walton is not coherent. On the other hand, we establish that two closely related connected graded rings are graded coherent. Finally, we prove that any exhaustively filtered ring is coherent if its Rees ring is graded coherent.

papers.title: Large orbits of $p$-groups on conjugacy classes of arbitrary finite groups
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27916v1

summary.background:
- Finite group: a group with finitely many elements, such as the symmetries of a finite object.
- p-group: a group whose size is a power of a prime p.
- Acting coprimely and faithfully: P applies symmetries to H in a way that is nontrivial and does not share prime factors with H's order in a problematic way.
- Conjugacy class: a set of elements of H that are equivalent under relabeling by H itself.
- Stabilizer / orbit: the stabilizer is the set of symmetries in P fixing a given class; the orbit is the set of classes it moves it to. Large orbit means small stabilizer.
- Solvable group: a group built up by stacking simple pieces that are abelian; nonsolvable groups contain more complex simple pieces.
- Classification of finite simple groups: a large completed classification of the basic building blocks of finite groups, used as a tool here.
- Irreducible character and inertia group: basic objects of representation theory; the inertia group is the set of symmetries that preserve a given character.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends a known result on large orbits of coprime p-group actions from solvable to arbitrary finite groups, showing via the classification of finite simple groups that some conjugacy class (or irreducible character) has stabilizer of order at most |P|^{1/2}, with a new nonsolvable family attaining the bound.
summary.plain: This paper is about symmetries of finite groups: a small group P of symmetries (of prime-power size) acts on a finite group H, and the question is how many elements of H P can leave mostly in place. The author-level result is that, for every such action, some conjugacy class of H has a stabilizer in P of size at most the square root of |P|. A previous paper had proved this only when H is solvable, and this paper removes that restriction, using the classification of finite simple groups.
summary.why: The bound is sharp: the text says it is attained, and the paper gives a new family of nonsolvable examples where it is reached. The result also gives, as a consequence, an irreducible character of H whose inertia group in P is small, which links the question to representation theory; the text does not say more about wider applications.

papers.abstract: Let $P$ be a $p$-group that acts faithfully and coprimely on a finite group $H$. In a previous paper it was shown that if $H$ is solvable, then there exists a conjugacy class $c$ of $H$ whose stabilizer in $P$ has order at most $|P|^{1/2}$, and that this bound is best possible. In this paper we remove the hypothesis that $H$ is solvable. As a consequence, there always exists an irreducible character of $H$ whose inertia group in $P$ has order at most $|P|^{1/2}$. The proof depends on the classification of finite simple groups. Its main new ingredient is a result on quasiprimitive linear actions of $p$-nilpotent groups which shows that the elements acting as field automorphisms can be ignored when one looks for vectors with small stabilizers. We also present a new family of examples, with nonsolvable $H$, in which the bound is attained.
